topic: Synthetic and naturally occurring polymers (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: Poly(ethene) and poly(propene) are made by addition polymerisation. Why are alkenes, rather than alkanes, used as the monomers?
items.correct: Alkenes contain a C=C bond that can open to make new bonds
items.misconception: Alkanes are saturated, so their molecules join end to end
items.why: 'Saturated' sounds like 'full', which students read as reactive or complete, rather than as having no double bond. Saturated means the molecule already holds as many hydrogen atoms as possible and has no C=C to open, so it cannot add on to another molecule.
items.random_wrong: Alkene molecules are held by weak intermolecular forces

items.q: Which monomer is used to make poly(propene)?
items.correct: Propene, because its molecules contain a C=C double bond
items.misconception: Propane, because the polymer chain is completely saturated
items.why: The finished polymer really is saturated, so students work backwards and choose the saturated starting material. The chain is saturated because the double bond of propene opened during polymerisation. The monomer itself must be the alkene.
items.random_wrong: Ethene, because n is a small number like three

items.q: What happens to the molecules in an addition polymerisation reaction?
items.correct: Many small monomers join into one large molecule
items.misconception: Monomers join and some atoms are lost
items.why: Chain-forming is imagined as requiring atoms to be removed, as in condensation polymerisation. Because no other molecule is formed, the mass of polymer equals the mass of monomer used.
items.random_wrong: Many monomers join and water molecules are given off

items.q: Which statement about a sample of poly(ethene) is correct?
items.correct: The chains are of many different lengths
items.misconception: Every chain holds the same number of units
items.why: Formulae usually describe one fixed molecule, so students expect a polymer to have one fixed size too. n is not a fixed number; a sample contains chains of many different lengths, all with the same repeating unit.
items.random_wrong: The units in a chain are held by weak forces

items.q: The specification gives the example n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)–n . What does this equation tell you?
items.correct: n ethene molecules give one chain of n repeating units
items.misconception: n ethene molecules give a polymer and n waters
items.why: Condensation polymerisation is met soon afterwards, and water loss is the memorable detail, so it gets attached to both types. In addition polymerisation nothing else is formed, which is exactly why the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer.
items.random_wrong: Two ethene molecules give a chain two units long

items.q: The repeating unit of poly(ethene) is –CH₂–CH₂–. Why does it contain the same atoms as the ethene monomer?
items.correct: Because no other molecule is formed in this reaction
items.misconception: Because the water that is lost is later taken back in
items.why: Condensation polymerisation is met soon afterwards, and water loss is the memorable detail, so it gets attached to both types. In addition polymerisation nothing else is formed, which is exactly why the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer.
items.random_wrong: Because two hydrogen atoms are lost from each end

items.q: 500 g of ethene is completely polymerised. Which statement about the atoms involved is correct?
items.correct: All the atoms end up in the poly(ethene) formed
items.misconception: Some atoms leave because a small molecule is released
items.why: Chain-forming is imagined as requiring atoms to be removed, as in condensation polymerisation. Because no other molecule is formed, the mass of polymer equals the mass of monomer used.
items.random_wrong: The polymer holds more carbon atoms per hydrogen

items.q: Which feature of a molecule shows that it can be a monomer for addition polymerisation?
items.correct: A carbon–carbon double bond
items.misconception: An –OH group on an end carbon
items.why: –OH is the functional group most recently learned in organic chemistry, so it is offered as the reactive group. For addition polymerisation the required functional group is C=C. An –OH group belongs to alcohols and to condensation monomers.
items.random_wrong: A fully saturated carbon chain

items.q: Which description is of an addition polymer rather than of a monomer?
items.correct: A repeating unit in brackets with bonds through them and n
items.misconception: A repeating unit in brackets with no bonds crossing them
items.why: Brackets elsewhere in chemistry enclose a finished group, so students close the unit off. The extension bonds are part of the required diagram: they show the unit is one link in a long chain.
items.random_wrong: A short molecule that holds just one C=C double bond

items.q: Chloroethene is CH₂=CHCl. Which description of the equation for its polymerisation is correct?
items.correct: n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets with n on the right
items.misconception: n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets plus n HCl given off
items.why: A chlorine atom is visible in the formula, so students expect it to be lost as HCl in the way water is lost elsewhere. The chlorine stays on the chain. Addition polymerisation joins the monomers with no other molecule formed.
items.random_wrong: n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets keeping the C=C

items.q: When the repeating unit of an addition polymer is drawn, why are bonds drawn through the brackets?
items.correct: To show more units are joined on both sides of it
items.misconception: To show the unit is a complete and separate molecule
items.why: Brackets elsewhere in chemistry enclose a finished group, so students close the unit off. The extension bonds are part of the required diagram: they show the unit is one link in a long chain.
items.random_wrong: To show where the double bond once was in the monomer

items.q: The repeating unit of a polymer is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. Which molecule was the monomer?
items.correct: Propene, since the C=C re-forms
items.misconception: Propane, as all bonds are single
items.why: The finished polymer really is saturated, so students work backwards and choose the saturated starting material. The chain is saturated because the double bond of propene opened during polymerisation. The monomer itself must be the alkene.
items.random_wrong: Butene, as the unit has 4 carbons

items.q: Tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂, undergoes addition polymerisation. What is the repeating unit of the polymer?
items.correct: –CF₂–CF₂– with the bonds drawn through the brackets
items.misconception: –CF₂=CF₂– with the double bond still in place
items.why: Students copy the monomer straight into the brackets without changing the bond, because the atoms are unchanged. The C=C is the bond that opens up to form the two new bonds to neighbouring units, so it can no longer be a double bond.
items.random_wrong: –CF₂–CF₂– without bonds through the brackets

items.q: What must a monomer have in order to take part in condensation polymerisation?
items.correct: Two functional groups in each monomer molecule
items.misconception: A carbon–carbon double bond in each of the monomers
items.why: Addition polymerisation is met first and the C=C rule is drilled, so it is carried over to every polymer. The C=C rule belongs only to addition polymerisation. Condensation monomers react through two functional groups instead.
items.random_wrong: One functional group at one end of a chain

items.q: Why is this type of polymerisation called condensation polymerisation?
items.correct: A small molecule such as water is lost each time
items.misconception: A gas condenses to a liquid as the polymer is made
items.why: The everyday meaning of condensation, from weather and windows, is far more familiar than the chemical one. Here condensation refers to the loss of a small molecule at each link, not to a change of state.
items.random_wrong: Steam given off turns back into liquid water

items.q: The simplest condensation polymers are made from two different monomers. What is true of those two monomers?
items.correct: Each has two of the same group
items.misconception: Each carries two different groups
items.why: Both polyesters and polypeptides are condensation polymers, and the two names get swapped. The link depends on the groups used. –OH with –COOH gives an ester link and so a polyester; –NH₂ with –COOH gives a polypeptide.
items.random_wrong: Each carries one group at an end

items.q: Ethanediol and hexanedioic acid are heated together. Which statement describes the polymerisation?
items.correct: The two different monomers join alternately, losing water
items.misconception: Many ethanediol molecules join each other, losing water
items.why: Addition polymers use a single monomer, so the same picture is applied to condensation polymers. An ester link needs an –OH group and a –COOH group, so the diol and the diacid must alternate along the chain.
items.random_wrong: The two monomers join with no other product formed

items.q: Which description of the monomer ethanediol is correct?
items.correct: Two carbon atoms, with an –OH group on each
items.misconception: Two carbon atoms, with a single –OH group on it
items.why: Ethanol is met first and looks similar; the '-diol' ending is not read as meaning two –OH groups. The 'di' in ethanediol tells you there are two –OH groups, which is what allows it to link at both ends.
items.random_wrong: Two carbon atoms, with a –COOH at each end

items.q: Hexanedioic acid is the second monomer used to make this polyester. Which description of it is correct?
items.correct: Six carbon atoms, with a –COOH group at each end
items.misconception: Six carbon atoms, with just one –COOH group on an end
items.why: Carboxylic acids are first met as one-ended molecules such as ethanoic acid, so that picture is reused. The 'dioic' ending shows two –COOH groups, one at each end, so the molecule can link on both sides.
items.random_wrong: Six carbon atoms, with an –OH group at either end

items.q: What is produced when ethanediol and hexanedioic acid polymerise together?
items.correct: A polyester and water molecules
items.misconception: A polyester and no other product
items.why: Addition polymerisation is met first and the C=C rule is drilled, so it is carried over to every polymer. The C=C rule belongs only to addition polymerisation. Condensation monomers react through two functional groups instead.
items.random_wrong: A polypeptide and water molecules

items.q: Amino acids can polymerise on their own, without a second kind of monomer. Why is this possible?
items.correct: Each molecule carries two different functional groups
items.misconception: Each molecule has two of the same functional group
items.why: The rule that condensation monomers carry two of the same group is learned for polyesters and then over-applied. Amino acids are the exception the specification highlights: the two groups are different, which is why one monomer can polymerise alone.
items.random_wrong: Each molecule has a carbon–carbon double bond

items.q: Glycine is H₂NCH₂COOH. Which groups react when glycine molecules polymerise, and what is lost?
items.correct: –NH₂ with –COOH, losing one water molecule
items.misconception: –NH₂ with –COOH, losing one ammonia molecule
items.why: The –NH₂ group is visible in the formula, so students expect the nitrogen-containing molecule to leave. The nitrogen stays in the chain. The H from –NH₂ and the OH from –COOH leave together as water.
items.random_wrong: Two –COOH groups, losing a water molecule

items.q: How does a protein differ from a polypeptide made from a single kind of amino acid?
items.correct: Different amino acids are combined in one chain
items.misconception: The same amino acid is repeated along the whole chain
items.why: Addition polymers use a single repeating unit, so that pattern is assumed to hold for every polymer. Proteins are built by combining different amino acids in one chain, which is what gives each protein its own properties.
items.random_wrong: Two separate chains are twisted round each other

items.q: Why is DNA described as essential for life?
items.correct: It encodes genetic instructions
items.misconception: It forms the plastic parts of cells
items.why: Polymers are introduced through poly(ethene) and plastics, so 'polymer' becomes a synonym for a synthetic material. A polymer is any very large molecule built from many monomers, whether it is made in a factory or in a cell.
items.random_wrong: It supplies the amino acids needed

items.q: Which statement describes the structure of most DNA molecules?
items.correct: Two polymer chains in the form of a double helix
items.misconception: One polymer chain coiled into a double helix
items.why: 'Double' is read as describing the coiling of one strand rather than the number of strands. The specification is explicit: most DNA molecules are two polymer chains in the form of a double helix.
items.random_wrong: Four polymer chains, one per type of nucleotide

items.q: Which list contains only naturally occurring polymers?
items.correct: DNA, proteins, starch and cellulose
items.misconception: DNA, proteins, starch and poly(ethene)
items.why: Polymers are introduced through poly(ethene) and plastics, so 'polymer' becomes a synonym for a synthetic material. A polymer is any very large molecule built from many monomers, whether it is made in a factory or in a cell.
items.random_wrong: DNA, glucose, starch and cellulose

items.q: Name the type of monomer from which both starch and cellulose are made.
items.correct: Glucose molecules build both these polymers
items.misconception: Amino acids build both of these long polymers
items.why: Amino acid is the biological monomer students recall most readily, so it is offered for every natural polymer. Both starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose; amino acids build proteins instead.
items.random_wrong: Starch molecules join together to make cellulose

items.q: Which statement correctly matches these naturally occurring polymers to their monomers?
items.correct: Proteins from amino acids; DNA from nucleotides
items.misconception: Proteins from nucleotides; DNA from the amino acids
items.why: DNA and proteins are both biological polymers met together, so their monomers get swapped. Amino acids build proteins. DNA is built from four different nucleotides.
items.random_wrong: Proteins from amino acids; DNA from glucose units

items.q: Ethanediol and hexanedioic acid polymerise. What is shown in the repeating unit of the polymer formed?
items.correct: An ester link, with bonds drawn through the brackets
items.misconception: An ester link, with the brackets closed off
items.why: Brackets elsewhere in chemistry enclose a finished group, so students close the unit off. The extension bonds are part of the required diagram: they show the unit is one link in a long chain.
items.random_wrong: A peptide link joining the two monomer units

items.q: Glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, polymerises to make a polypeptide. What is the repeating unit of that polypeptide?
items.correct: –NH–CH₂–CO– with bonds through the brackets
items.misconception: –NH₂–CH₂–COOH– with bonds through the brackets
items.why: The rule that the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer is learned for addition polymers and then applied to condensation polymers as well. That rule holds only when no other molecule is formed. In condensation polymerisation water is lost at every link, so those atoms are not in the repeating unit.
items.random_wrong: –O–CH₂–CO– with bonds through the brackets

items.q: Which molecule is the monomer for poly(ethene)?
items.correct: Ethene, CH₂=CH₂, which contains a C=C double bond.
items.misconception: Poly(ethene) is made from ethane, because ethane is the familiar two-carbon hydrocarbon and the names sound the same.
items.why: 'Ethene' and 'ethane' differ by one letter and sound almost identical when spoken, and alkanes are taught first. Only alkenes make addition polymers. Ethane, C₂H₆, has only single bonds, so nothing can open up and it cannot polymerise.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the repeating unit contain the same atoms as the monomer?
items.correct: Yes, exactly the same atoms in the same numbers.
items.misconception: Atoms are lost from the monomer as the chain forms, so the repeating unit is smaller than the monomer.
items.why: Students assume that joining molecules must cost something, by analogy with condensation reactions. No other molecule is formed, so every atom of every monomer ends up in the polymer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does n stand for in n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)–n ?
items.correct: A very large number of monomer molecules, and the same number of repeating units.
items.misconception: n stands for a small fixed number such as two or three.
items.why: Balanced equations normally use small whole numbers, so a letter is read as standing in for one. A polymer chain contains thousands of repeating units; n is a large, unspecified number that is the same on both sides.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What holds the monomer units together in a polymer chain?
items.correct: Strong covalent bonds formed when the C=C opens.
items.misconception: The units are held to each other by intermolecular forces.
items.why: Intermolecular forces are used to explain the properties of polymers, so students apply them to the chain itself. Within a chain the units are joined by covalent bonds; intermolecular forces act only between separate chains.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a monomer with only one functional group form a polymer?
items.correct: No. It could react once and then the chain would stop.
items.misconception: One functional group per monomer is enough to build a long chain.
items.why: Students think about a single reaction between two molecules and do not picture the chain having to grow at both ends. Two functional groups are needed so that each monomer can join on both sides and the chain can keep growing.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which small molecule is lost when a polyester forms?
items.correct: Water.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is given off when the monomers join.
items.why: Acids are associated with giving off carbon dioxide from carbonate reactions, so that product is recalled. The –OH and the –COOH group combine, and the atoms removed are H and OH, which form water.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many different nucleotides build DNA?
items.correct: Four.
items.misconception: There are two different nucleotides, one for each chain.
items.why: The double helix has two strands, and that number is transferred to the number of monomers. There are four different nucleotides; the two chains are made from the same set of four.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is glucose a polymer?
items.correct: No. Glucose is a monomer.
items.misconception: Glucose belongs in a list of naturally occurring polymers.
items.why: Glucose is met alongside starch and cellulose in biology, so it is grouped with them without checking the size. Glucose is a small molecule and is the monomer; starch and cellulose are the polymers made from it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is cellulose made from?
items.correct: Glucose monomers.
items.misconception: Natural polymers are built by joining smaller polymers together — for example, cellulose is made by joining starch molecules.
items.why: Starch and cellulose are met as a pair, so one is assumed to be built from the other. Starch and cellulose are two different polymers, each built directly from glucose monomers.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is DNA described as having four different monomers?
items.correct: Because four different nucleotides are used to build the chains.
items.misconception: There is one polymer chain for each of the four nucleotides.
items.why: The words 'four' and 'two' both appear in the description, so the numbers are attached to the wrong things. Most DNA molecules have two chains, and each chain is built from a sequence of the four different nucleotides.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.7.3 Synthetic and naturally occurring polymers (chemistry only)
